title: Scion Brand Returns with U.S.-Built Kei Trucks
summary: Toyota’s affordable sub-brand revives with micro trucks for fleets and beyond. The post Scion Brand Returns with U.S.-Built Kei Trucks appeared first on Shop Press .
body_markdown:
It’s not often that a car brand comes back from the dead.


In a surprise move, Toyota has revived its Scion sub-brand for the United States. No mention of sport coupes or boxy hatchbacks this time, though. Instead, “Scion by Toyota” will be selling kei trucks, manufactured at a plant in Indiana and other Toyota U.S. facilities. What’s the deal, and who will be able to buy these little trucks?


Scion Kei Truck 2027-03. Photo: Toyota Photo.


### Kei Details


We haven’t heard a peep out of Scion in the decade since the brand folded up at the end of 2016. The “new” Scion is sticking close to its old positioning in the automotive marketplace: affordable, practical transportation aimed at price-conscious buyers.


This time around, Scion is focused on fleets instead of young drivers. Parent company Toyota sees growing demand for compact, efficient vehicles, and kei trucks might just fill a gap in the market. Until now, the main obstacle for kei-class vehicles has been the hassle of importing them. Manufacturing the micro trucks here in the States bypasses the trouble of importing and getting foreign-market vehicles approved for legal use on public U.S. roads. The new truck production line is “…supported by a $34 million investment that will add approximately 50 new jobs,” says Toyota’s press release.


“Assembly at Toyota Indiana represents the company’s continued commitment to investing in the U.S. and American jobs. The investment will establish new vehicle assembly operations and upgrade production and logistics infrastructure, bringing this unique utility vehicle closer to U.S. customers.”


2027 Scion KEI-01. Photo: Toyota Photo.


### Meet the KEI-01


There’s just one vehicle in the Scion catalog for now. It’s called, fittingly, the KEI-01. Our international readers might recognize it as a rebranded Daihatsu Hijet or Toyota Pixis. Standard trim is a 660 cc three-cylinder engine with a CVT and 4WD. These are famously tough little trucks, but there’s one major drawback for many U.S. customers. The speed will top out at 25mph to comply with federal Low-Speed Vehicle (LSV) requirements. This positions the KEI-01 somewhere between light pickup trucks and utility SxS vehicles like Mules and Gators.


Scion’s betting that fleets will like the low cost, high versatility, and bare minimum running gear to operate legally on the street. City/municipal governments, campuses, parks, work crews, urban delivery services, and farms would all be examples of customers who might want a mighty mini hauler or ten. Given the differences between the kei truck’s mechanicals and the rest of Toyota’s lineup, it might be for the best that initial sales are limited to fleets. North American techs won’t have much experience with this platform unless they’ve already worked as kei specialists.


### Consumer Sales Next?


What about the rest of us? If fleet demand takes off, “Scion by Toyota” has indicated that limited sales to the public might open up. The fleet keis will be sold through select Toyota dealers, which is nearly the same piggyback strategy we saw from Scion last time. Don’t call it a comeback, but interest in small, useful vehicles is running high in the U.S., and Scion could be well-positioned to meet demand from kei enthusiasts. The sub-brand also announced concepts for an electric scooter and an aggressive turbo SxS, so it seems like they’re still exploring their options.


So, what’s your take? Is the KEI-01 too small and slow to be more than a niche oddity? Or is the market ready for inexpensive, barebones transportation, especially in urban areas where parking is tight and speed limits are low?


We’ll find out soon enough. KEI-01 trucks will be available for fleet purchase starting in 2027.
